blocks.text: Core objective: Distinguish ovulation induction from ovarian stimulation and IUI, select suitable patients, explain the treatment pathway and recognise complications.

items.text: Ovulation induction: Use of medication to stimulate ovulation in a woman who does not ovulate regularly.
Ovarian stimulation: Use of medication to encourage follicular development, often to produce more than one follicle during fertility treatment.
IUI: Placement of prepared sperm directly into the uterine cavity around the time of ovulation.
Timed intercourse: Intercourse planned around the fertile window.
Follicular monitoring: Assessment of follicle development, usually with transvaginal ultrasound and sometimes hormonal tests.
Trigger injection: Medication used to induce final oocyte maturation and help time ovulation or a fertility procedure.

blocks.text: These terms are related but not interchangeable. Ovulation induction may be used with timed intercourse, while IUI additionally involves laboratory preparation of sperm and intrauterine placement.
Before recommending ovulation induction or IUI, establish the likely cause of infertility.

blocks.text: Other investigations are selected according to the history and clinical findings. Avoid ordering every hormonal test indiscriminately.
OSCE pearl: Assess both partners in parallel. Do not repeatedly induce ovulation without checking whether other major infertility factors are present.
Ovulation induction is used principally when ovulatory dysfunction is contributing to infertility, including:

items.text: Anovulation associated with PCOS.
Selected cases of hypothalamic ovulatory dysfunction after appropriate assessment.
Other treatable causes of ovulatory dysfunction, once the underlying problem has been addressed.

blocks.text: It is not routinely required in women who already ovulate normally unless there is a separate treatment indication.
A. Letrozole
An aromatase inhibitor that temporarily reduces oestrogen production, leading to increased endogenous gonadotrophin stimulation.
It is generally the preferred first-line medication for ovulation induction in anovulatory infertility associated with PCOS, when appropriate and where pregnancy has been excluded before treatment.
B. Clomiphene citrate
A selective oestrogen receptor modulator that reduces oestrogen-mediated negative feedback, increasing pituitary gonadotrophin release.
It is an alternative where letrozole is unsuitable or unavailable, depending on the clinical context and local guidance.
C. Gonadotrophins
Injectable FSH, sometimes combined with LH activity, directly stimulates follicular development.

These are used in selected patients when oral treatment is unsuccessful or when the clinical indication warrants them. They require careful monitoring because of the risk of multiple pregnancy and OHSS.
D. hCG trigger
Mimics the LH surge and promotes final oocyte maturation.
It may be used when follicular development is appropriate, but the decision must account for the number of follicles and OHSS risk.

blocks.text: Letrozole is used off-label for ovulation induction in some jurisdictions. Follow local protocols and product guidance. Medication choice, dose and duration must be individualised by the treating clinician.

subsections.subsection_title: 6. Step-by-step ovulation induction with timed intercourse

blocks.text: This is a typical pathway, not a prescription for an individual patient.

items.text: Confirm anovulation and assess infertility factors. Establish the diagnosis and assess pregnancy status, semen parameters and tubal factors as indicated.
Exclude pregnancy and review contraindications. Review medications, relevant medical conditions and any risk factors requiring specialist input.
Start the prescribed ovulation-induction medication. Treatment is generally scheduled early in the menstrual cycle according to the chosen protocol.
Monitor the response when indicated. Ultrasound assesses follicular development; monitoring intensity depends on the medication and the patient's risk profile.
Identify the fertile window. Use the prescribed monitoring method, ovulation-prediction approach or trigger protocol.
Advise timed intercourse. Provide clear instructions based on the anticipated ovulation time.
Arrange pregnancy testing and follow-up. Test at the recommended time and reassess treatment response before any subsequent cycle.

content_groups.group_title: What if ovulation does not occur?

items.text: Check adherence, cycle timing and whether the diagnosis is correct.
Review the response to treatment and investigate relevant endocrine causes.
Reassess the treatment protocol under clinical supervision.
Consider specialist-directed alternative treatment if an appropriate response is not achieved.

blocks.text: Avoid repeated dose escalation without reviewing the cause of treatment failure and the risk of multifollicular development.

IUI involves introducing prepared sperm into the uterine cavity using a fine catheter around the time of ovulation. It bypasses the cervix but does not bypass the fallopian tubes; fertilisation usually still occurs within a tube.

blocks.title: IUI may be considered for selected patients with:

items.text: Unexplained infertility, after appropriate assessment and discussion of alternatives.
Mild male-factor infertility in suitable circumstances.
Difficulty with intercourse or ejaculation when sperm can be collected and appropriately prepared.
Use of donor sperm where permitted and appropriate.
Selected cases in which ovulation induction and insemination are planned together.

blocks.text: Suitability depends on the overall fertility evaluation, including tubal patency and semen parameters after preparation.

content_groups.group_title: When is IUI unsuitable or less appropriate?

items.text: Bilateral complete tubal obstruction.
Severe male-factor infertility where adequate prepared sperm cannot be obtained for IUI.
Untreated active genital tract infection.
Other clinical circumstances in which a different fertility treatment is more appropriate.

blocks.text: In significant tubal disease or severe male-factor infertility, IVF, sometimes with ICSI, may be more suitable.

Confirm timing. IUI is scheduled around spontaneous or medication-triggered ovulation, according to the clinic protocol.
Collect the semen sample. The sample is obtained according to laboratory instructions, with correct identification and handling.
Prepare the sperm. The laboratory processes the sample to select suitable motile sperm and remove seminal plasma and other unwanted components.
Position the patient. Usually supine, with a speculum used to visualise the cervix.
Introduce the catheter. A fine insemination catheter is passed gently through the cervix into the uterine cavity.
Instil the prepared sperm. The sample is introduced slowly according to the clinical protocol.
Remove the catheter and observe the patient. The procedure is usually brief; assess discomfort or vasovagal symptoms.
Give aftercare instructions. Explain the pregnancy-test date, medication plan and symptoms requiring medical attention.

blocks.text: Routine bed rest after IUI has not been shown to be necessary. Follow the fertility centre's instructions.
IUI is performed close to ovulation, but exact timing varies with the treatment protocol.

blocks.text: When a trigger is used, insemination is generally scheduled within the following day or two according to the clinic's protocol.
Exam point: Do not give a universal exact timing without knowing whether ovulation is spontaneous or triggered and which protocol is being followed.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Complications of ovulation induction and IUI

blocks.text: More than one follicle may ovulate, resulting in twins or higher-order pregnancy.

items.text: Preterm birth.
Low birth weight.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Gestational diabetes.
Increased neonatal morbidity.

blocks.text: Prevention involves appropriate medication selection, monitoring and avoiding insemination or advising abstinence/barrier protection according to the clinic's protocol if the follicular response creates an unacceptable multiple-pregnancy risk.
OHSS is especially relevant with gonadotrophin stimulation and certain trigger strategies. It is less common with oral agents but is not impossible in all circumstances.

items.text: Marked abdominal bloating or pain.
Persistent vomiting.
Rapid weight gain.
Reduced urine output.
Breathlessness or faintness.

blocks.text: Severe symptoms require urgent assessment.

rows: May occur around ovulation or during follicular stimulation
Uncommon but possible following an intrauterine procedure
Repeated unsuccessful cycles can be difficult

blocks.text: PCOS is a common cause of anovulatory infertility. Management should address reproductive goals as well as general metabolic health.

items.text: Confirm the diagnosis and exclude alternative causes of irregular ovulation where appropriate.
Assess weight, blood pressure and metabolic risk factors.
Offer preconception advice, including folic acid according to local guidance, smoking cessation and review of medication safety.
Assess the partner and other fertility factors rather than assuming PCOS is the only cause.
Offer letrozole as first-line pharmacological ovulation induction when appropriate.
Monitor treatment response and review unsuccessful cycles.
Refer for specialist fertility treatment when indicated.

blocks.text: Lifestyle support may improve general health and metabolic outcomes. It should be offered respectfully and should not be used to shame patients or delay appropriate fertility care.

blocks.title: Depending on the patient's circumstances, a specialist may consider:

items.text: Reviewing the diagnosis and adherence.
Alternative oral ovulation-induction strategies.
Gonadotrophins with careful monitoring.
Laparoscopic ovarian surgery in selected cases.
IVF when other options are unsuitable or unsuccessful.

blocks.text: The sequence is individualised rather than rigid.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. What if the patient has hypothalamic amenorrhoea?

blocks.text: Functional hypothalamic amenorrhoea may be associated with low energy availability, excessive exercise, psychological stress or significant weight loss. Other causes must be excluded.
Management focuses on correcting the underlying energy imbalance or contributing condition. If pregnancy is desired and ovulation does not return, specialist fertility care may be required.

Gonadotrophin treatment or pulsatile GnRH may be considered in suitable patients depending on availability and local expertise. This differs from treating PCOS, where the underlying hormonal physiology is different.
Example OSCE response
“Your investigations suggest that IUI may be an option if at least one fallopian tube is open and the sperm sample is suitable after preparation.

“The procedure involves collecting a semen sample, preparing it in the laboratory and placing the selected sperm through a thin catheter into the uterus around the time of ovulation. It is usually brief and does not normally require anaesthesia.
“Possible risks include mild cramping, a small risk of infection, ectopic pregnancy and, if medication is used to stimulate several follicles, multiple pregnancy and ovarian hyperstimulation.

“IUI does not guarantee pregnancy, and its success depends on factors such as age, the cause of infertility and sperm parameters. We will discuss whether IUI or another option is most appropriate for you.”
Q1. What is the difference between ovulation induction and ovarian stimulation?

Ovulation induction aims to achieve ovulation in someone who does not ovulate regularly. Ovarian stimulation aims to develop follicles and may intentionally produce more than one mature follicle, depending on the treatment.
Q2. Which drug is generally first-line for anovulatory infertility due to PCOS?
Letrozole is generally first-line when appropriate and when other major infertility factors have been assessed.
Q3. What is the mechanism of letrozole?
It inhibits aromatase, temporarily reducing oestrogen synthesis and increasing endogenous gonadotrophin stimulation through reduced negative feedback.
Q4. Why is tubal patency important before IUI?
IUI places sperm inside the uterus but does not bypass the tubes. At least one functionally patent tube is generally needed for natural fertilisation.
Q5. Why is semen preparation performed before IUI?
It selects suitable motile sperm and removes seminal plasma and other components that should not be introduced into the uterine cavity in an unprocessed sample.
Q6. What is the most important complication of multifollicular stimulation?
Multiple pregnancy is a major concern; OHSS is another important complication, particularly with gonadotrophin-based treatment.
Q7. What would you do if ultrasound shows too many developing follicles before IUI?
The treating team reassesses the risk of multiple pregnancy and may cancel the cycle, withhold the trigger or advise avoiding unprotected intercourse according to the clinic protocol.
Q8. Is IUI appropriate for bilateral tubal obstruction?
Generally no, because sperm and oocytes still need to meet in a fallopian tube. IVF may be appropriate because it bypasses the tubes.
Q9. Can IUI treat severe male-factor infertility?
Often not effectively. IVF with ICSI may be more suitable depending on the semen findings and whether usable sperm can be obtained.
Q10. What should you do if a patient has visual disturbances while taking clomiphene?
Advise the patient to stop further doses pending prompt clinical assessment and contact the treating clinician, because visual symptoms are a significant adverse effect requiring evaluation.
Q11. Does ovulation induction guarantee pregnancy?
No. Ovulation may occur without fertilisation, implantation or a live birth. The underlying cause and other fertility factors remain important.
Q12. When should a pregnancy test be performed after IUI?
At the time advised by the fertility clinic, commonly around two weeks after insemination depending on the protocol. Testing too early can give misleading results.
